blogs.title: The Speculative Chain: Why Procedural Rights Don't Confer Standing Without Concrete Harm
blogs.description: This post analyzes the D.C. Circuit's rigorous application of *Lujan* and recent Supreme Court precedents (*Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine*, *Haaland*) regarding causation and redressability. It focuses on why the court rejected AFL's argument that a mandatory statutory duty to investigate translates into standing when the link to the ultimate relief (FOIA disclosure) relies on a multi-step chain of discretionary decisions by non-parties.

blogs.title: Investigation vs. Information: The Limits of 'Informational Injury' in Administrative Law
blogs.description: Focusing on the second prong of AFL's standing claim, this article examines the distinction between a statutory right to demand an administrative investigation and a statutory right to receive specific information *about* that investigation. It explores how the court clarified that without a clear congressional mandate for notice-and-comment style transparency in OSC investigations, plaintiffs cannot manufacture 'informational injury' merely by being excluded from an internal inquiry process.

blogs.title: Enforcement Discretion and the Wall of Article III: Reaffirming *Heckler v. Chaney*
blogs.description: This commentary discusses the court's reliance on *Heckler v. Chaney* to explain why federal courts cannot compel an executive agency (like the Office of Special Counsel) to exercise its enforcement discretion, even when statutes use mandatory language ('shall'). The post argues that this ruling reinforces a critical boundary in administrative law: while Congress can create duties, it cannot easily bypass Article III limits by forcing agencies into litigation where their primary function remains discretionary enforcement.
